On a set schedule the system automatically looks for a more robust version of every strategy running in paper trading:
  1. Generate candidates: fine-tune parameters around the current strategy (MA periods, thresholds, stop-loss/take-profit, timeframe) in two search rounds, up to 120 candidates; optionally plus 1 DeepSeek suggestion.
  2. Robustness score: training set only (one year), split into 4 quarters. Score = average quarterly return − 0.5 × quarterly return volatility − 0.25 × max drawdown. Candidates with too few trades are dropped. Only those at least 1 point above the current version move on.
  3. Hold-out check: compare with the current version on data the candidate has never "seen" (latest market data first, the validation set if that's not enough, at most 3 times per strategy). The candidate must trade, return no less than the current version and not draw down noticeably deeper. The independent test set is never used.
  4. Auto-replace: once it passes, it is frozen as a new version; paper trading switches when flat, or after the current position is sold. Every step is logged.
  5. Challenger live run: if hold-out history isn't enough to decide, the candidate isn't thrown away — it becomes a "challenger" running side by side with the incumbent on live data from the moment it's registered, evaluated hourly; after the minimum days, if it's no worse than the incumbent → automatically promoted and deployed to paper trading; clearly worse → dropped. US ETF timing parameters evolve the same way.
Reminder: more robust in the past ≠ guaranteed profit in the future. This process keeps weeding out clearly worse versions and leaves verifiable evidence for every replacement; it cannot guarantee profit.
